c.v: This stage turns the failures we produced by hand into a suite that runs them without us. Every check in the bench had been proved once, at a keyboard: we ran the missing-odometry scenario with the relay switched off, raised the supervisor's odometry timeout to five seconds, and watched the right line of the verdict fail each time. A proof you have to repeat by hand is not a net.

The decision worth defending is that half the suite expects failure. A suite that runs only the happy path tells you the robot still works and nothing about whether the checks are still watching it, so each case carries an expectation: this one passes, or this one fails and this named check is the one that fails. The comparison lives in
, tested like the rest of it, and the shell script does nothing but run scenarios and hand over files.

What we can now show: one command runs five cases, prints a line each, and exits non-zero when any expectation is unmet. Breaking the supervisor again turns one line red without anyone having to remember what to look at.

c.v: Three of those deserve a place in a suite and three do not, and the rule is worth stating before you choose. A failure earns a test when it would be silent if it came back, when it fails for one nameable reason, and when running it costs less than the damage of missing it. The robot moved by hand fails the first part of that: it needs a person to drag a model, so it is a checklist item for the milestone review rather than a test. A drive speed of zero fails the second: it breaks everything at once and tells you nothing the other cases do not.

A case is three facts about a verdict file: its name, whether the run should pass, and, when it should fail, which check should be the failing one. That last part is what makes the suite worth having. A case that only asks for

c.v: Three passing and two failing is the shape to aim for. The passing ones say the robot still does its job; the failing ones say the checks still notice when it does not.

blocks.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# run_regressions.sh: runs every case in cases.txt and reports which met its expectation.
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
source install/setup.bash
set -euo pipefail
trim() { sed 's/^[[:space:]]*//; s/[[:space:]]*$//' <<< "$1"; }
mkdir -p results/regression
met=0
total=0
while IFS='|' read -r name scenario expect failing arguments; do
  name=$(trim "$name"); scenario=$(trim "$scenario"); expect=$(trim "$expect")
  failing=$(trim "$failing"); arguments=$(trim "$arguments")
  total=$((total + 1))
  ./run_scenario.sh "$scenario" $arguments > "results/regression/$name.log" 2>&1 || true
  cp "results/$scenario.txt" "results/regression/$name.txt" 2>/dev/null || true
  if install/bench_core/bin/check_verdict "$name" "$expect" "$failing" "results/regression/$name.txt"; then
    met=$((met + 1))
  fi
done < <(grep -v '^[[:space:]]*\(#\|$\)' cases.txt)
echo "$met of $total cases met their expectation"
test "$met" -eq "$total"

c.v: Three lines in it are deliberate.
is unquoted, because it has to split into separate launch arguments or vanish when it is empty, and it is the one place in the bench where word splitting is wanted.
after each run keeps the loop going, since a case that is supposed to fail makes
exit 1 and that is the expected outcome, not an error. And the copy has its own
, because a launch that never wrote a verdict is a result the tool reports rather than a crash of the script.

Write down the wall time of the whole suite and of the slowest case. That number is the decision: a suite of a few minutes runs on every push, and one of twenty runs at night with a link to the report in the morning. The CI topic spends that number; this topic's job is to measure it. Note also that every case calls
, which starts the world, so the suite is bounded by Gazebo starting five times rather than by anything the bench does.

c.v: Two things happen, and both are worth seeing.
measures that promise directly and needs no simulator. The suite goes red a few minutes later on
the verdict came out the other way round
, which now meets its expectation for the wrong reason. Put the default back and run both again.

That pair is the argument for having two layers. The unit test tells you in seconds which promise you broke; the scenario suite tells you that the robot in the world behaves the way the promise claims. Neither replaces the other, and the fast one is the one you run on every save.
